title: Compact kernel routing: mixed-quant execution path and KV-aware scheduling spec
content:
Background and purpose:

This document defines a compact, pragmatic execution path for mixed-precision and mixed-format quantized models that we will use inside the serving runtime. It focuses on kernel selection and routing constraints across INT8, FP8, GPTQ, and AWQ formats and how those choices interact with the KV cache, continuous batching, and scheduling heuristics. The goal is to provide an actionable runtime contract: what kernels are allowed for each operator/layer, how memory must be laid out, how to detect incompatibilities and fall back, and what metrics to expose during rollouts. This is a working spec (draft) intended to be conservative and deployable incrementally.

High-level goals:
- Correctness: avoid silent numerical catastrophes when mixing quant formats or switching kernels at runtime.
- Determinism: given identical inputs+model version, inference must be bitwise deterministic when using the same kernel path.
- Low-latency SLO compliance: prefer low-overhead kernel switches and avoid KV cache thrash that increases p50/p95 latency.
- Memory efficiency: support compact packed weight representations while keeping alignment constraints simple for device code.
- Incremental rollout: provide clear signals and safe fallbacks to FP16/FP32 when quantized path is unsafe or missing.

Scope and non-goals:
- We do not redesign quant training or model conversion flows here. Assume model conversion produced metadata describing weight layout, scale tensors, and quant type per-layer.
- We do not cover multi-GPU model parallel kernel placement in depth; interaction notes are included but detailed MP mapping is out of scope.

Terminology:
- Kernel variant: device implementation for an operator (e.g., matmul) specialized to a quant format and micro-optimizations (INT8-symmetric-fast, AWQ-block-16, FP8-e5m2-fused).
- Execution path: sequence of kernel variants selected at runtime for the model graph.
- Compatibility token: small runtime tag derived from model metadata that kernels use to check layout/scale/bitwidth compatibility with cached KV entries.

Constraints by quant type:
1) INT8 (per-channel, symmetric or asymmetric):
- Weight layout: channel-major packing (C-out aligned to 32) with optional 4x/8x blocking for tensor cores.
- Scale storage: per-channel FP16 or FP32 scale tensor allowed; INT8 kernels must accept either and internally widen scale to FP32 for accumulation.
- Kernel precondition: input activation type must be FP16 or FP32 unless a dequant kernel (act-deq) is used; runtime must detect and insert dequant if needed (cost: ~0.2ms for 1k tokens on V100-class).
- KV cache: INT8 matmul kernels must be able to consume cached KV in FP16; if model cache produced in FP16, runtime must not accept INT8 kernels that assume compacted (quantized) KV without explicit reformatting.

2) FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2 variants):
- Weight layout: packed bytes with exponent bias recorded in metadata. Alignment: 256-bit lanes recommended to maximize vectorization.
- Dynamic range: FP8 kernels must provide a runtime guard to detect exponent saturation patterns on a layer-by-layer basis (e.g., histogram of exponents across first N tokens). If saturation > threshold (config default 0.5%), mark layer unsafe and route to FP16 fallback.
- KV cache: FP8 cached KV entries must carry an explicit exponent-bias field. If mismatch with kernel expectation occurs, runtime must either rebase (costly) or fall back to FP16 path.

3) GPTQ / AWQ (post-training quantized formats):
- GPTQ: per-tensor scale + small correction terms. Kernels must read an auxiliary correction buffer when present; ABI must include pointer+length for corrections.
- AWQ: block-wise adaptive scale and integer weights stored in 4-bit/3-bit compressions. Kernel constraints: block size encoded in metadata, kernels must support direct bit-extraction or runtime unpacking. Runtime should prefer kernels that can operate on packed AWQ without full unpacking to avoid memory pressure.
- Determinism: GPTQ/AWQ kernels must support a deterministic accumulation order; non-deterministic atomics are disallowed for these paths.

Runtime ABI and kernel contract:
- Every kernel variant must accept a small header (Compatibility token) with these fields (flat struct): model_version, layer_id, weight_format_id, scale_pointer, scale_dtype, kv_cache_format, block_size_flags, reserved. This header is a contiguous byte array (<=64 bytes) passed to device kernels via uniform/registers.
- Kernel must validate header and return an explicit status code (OK | INCOMPATIBLE | NUMERIC_RISK). INCOMPATIBLE triggers scheduler-level retry with alternate kernel. NUMERIC_RISK causes metrics logging and optional canary fallback depending on rollout policy.
- Memory alignment: weight buffers must be 256-bit aligned. Packed AWQ/GPTQ correction buffers must be 128-bit aligned. Device code may assume these constraints.

KV cache coherence and layout constraints:
- Canonical on-device cache format is FP16 KV for host-managed (default) deployments. Quantized-on-disk cache (e.g., stored AWQ/INT8) requires on-load reformatting to canonical format before first use OR must be accompanied by kernel that can consume quantized KV with an explicit header.
- Cache replacement: when a kernel requires a rebase (e.g., FP8 exponent rebase) the runtime MUST snapshot eviction candidates and prefer evicting cold keys (LRU) to make room for rebased entries. Rebase operations are rate-limited per-model to avoid sudden bandwidth storms.
- KV alignment: cached KV blocks must be contiguous in memory for the layer and aligned to 64B. This enables DMA-friendly device copies and reduces fragmentation.

Scheduler interactions and continuous batching implications:
- Kernel switching cost: switching kernel variants for a model between batches has a fixed penalty (meta-estimated per device; default 0.6ms for A100-class) due to microkernel context warmups and potential reformatting. Scheduler must account for this when grouping requests by model+kernel compatibility token.
- Batching policy: group requests by compatibility token first, then affinity (same model version), then latency priority. This minimizes reformat/rebase and KV incoherence. In practice, a token-aware batching window of 3–6ms yields best p95 improvements for mixed-precision fleets.
- Canary routing: enable N% of traffic on new quant kernel (default 1%) and capture both per-layer numeric diagnostic metrics and overall latency/cost deltas. Canary failures: if NUMERIC_RISK counts exceed threshold (default 100 events/hour) or p95 latency increases > 10% for the canary group, rollback automatically.

Fallback heuristics and safe modes:
- Deterministic fallback chain for each layer: best_quant_kernel -> mixed_precision_kernel (dequant/accumulate FP16) -> FP16 fused kernel -> FP32 (slow) fallback.
- Automatic triggers: kernel returns INCOMPATIBLE -> immediate retry with fallback chain. NUMERIC_RISK -> sample N inputs across T seconds (default N=10 over 60s); if risk persists, promote to deterministic fallback and emit alert.
- Graceful degradation: when a model sees repeated rebase churn (e.g., constant KV exponent rebasing), throttle low-priority traffic on that model and schedule background rebases during off-peak.

Metrics and observability:
- Per-layer exposure: kernel_variant, compatibility_token, numeric_risk_count, incompatibility_count, rebase_ops_count, avg_kernel_switch_cost_ms, p50/p95/p99 latency by kernel_variant.
- Alerts: elevated numeric_risk_count, repeated rebase_ops_count above threshold, p95 latency regression for canary vs baseline.
- Debug traces: sample raw exponent histograms (FP8) and weight-correction residuals (GPTQ) for triage. These are collected only in canary/diagnostic mode to limit telemetry.

Rollout plan and tests:
- Unit tests: kernel ABI conformance, header mismatch injection tests, simulated KV formats.
- Integration tests: synthetic models exercising INT8->FP16 fallback, FP8 saturation detection (inject synthetic high-magnitude activations), AWQ block unpack path.
- Canary: 1% traffic for 24h with baseline comparison. If pass, 10% for 48h, then 100% with monitoring retention on per-layer metrics for 7d.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Should the canonical on-device KV always be FP16 or allow FP8 canonical for extreme memory savings? (FP16 chosen as default because FP8 rebases are frequent for some workloads.)
- How aggressive should auto-rebasing be vs falling back? Rebase costs vary wildly by device and network topology; need empirical thresholds per-host-type.
- MP mapping: when model is sharded, some kernels may be unavailable on a shard; scheduler policy for cross-shard fallback needs a separate spec.

Appendix: quick examples
- Example 1: Transformer with AWQ weights on attention and FP8 for feed-forward. Runtime loads weights for attention with header indicating AWQ-block-16; selects awq-block16-kernel that consumes packed KV only if canonical KV format is "AWQ-packed"; otherwise runtime repacks KV into packed form and logs rebase cost.
- Example 2: Decoder-only model converted to FP8-e5m2. After first tokens, exponent histogram shows >1% saturation on layer 6 -> runtime marks layer 6 as unsafe and routes to FP16 fused matmul for subsequent requests; telemetry records numeric_risk_count and canary flag.

Next steps and owners:
- PK: implement header validation and status codes in device ABI (owner: Diego Ramos, due 2025-05-05).
- Scheduler: token-aware batching window and kernel-switch cost model (owner: Maya Lin, due 2025-05-12).
- Bench: measure kernel_switch_cost for A100, H100, and consumer GPUs (owner: Connor McBride, due 2025-05-19).

References:
- INF-2873 (linked), runtime PR #4210 (linked), internal quant conversion notes (confluence id: QCONV-114).

This spec is intentionally conservative: prefer clear safety signals and workloads that can be rolled forward incrementally. Feedback welcome — add comments in the PR or tag the doc owner.
